questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
The aspects that were of primary concern to me were the following:

1) Opportunity to improve my Italian
2) High level of education at host university
3) Academic tradition for nurturing the humanities at the host university

As the oldest university in the western world (founded 1088), University of Bologna satisfied the above three aspects. The university has long cultivated the humanities, offering a wide range of courses within the arts and humanties. Furthermore, University of Bologna is known as one of the best universities in Italy, as they pride themselves of upholding a high academic level for longer than any other university in the Western world. Needless to say Bologna offered me the opportunity to take all my lectures in Italian so that I could improve my English language skills. The language school that is connected with the university also offered Italian courses with an intensive course placed right before the beginning of the semester, which was ideal for preparing me for my exchange.
For me it was also an advantage for the University of Bologna that Bologna primarily is a university city. Unlike universities in Rome, Milan or other Italian metropoles, in which the university is just one institution out of countless, the university in Bologna is the most important institution of the city: it is both a pride and a priority of the city.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was extremely easy to find the necessary information. The website of the University of Bologna provides all the information that is needed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I do not remember needing any assistance upon arrival.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: The university of Bologna offer a website (SAIS) that can be used for finding student housing in Bologna.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The main regret for me is that the website (SAIS) recommended by the university is used primarily by international students, which means it is difficult to find Italian flatmates. I ended up living with German, Dutch and Iranian students. I should have preferred to have lived with Italian students. It is worthwhile to keep in mind when looking for accommodation that the flatmates might be international like yourselves!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The housing in Bologna is extremely expensive. The city must do more to build student accommodation so as to increase the offers for students.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: On the website of the university there is a page dedicated to exchange students. Through the website it is possible to book an appointment for what they call a "check-in". The check-in happens online with verification of ID. After check-in has been completed, the student receives a QR-code to print a student card at machines on campus.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There is an international desk available, which can be contacted in person or by email (they usual respond within 24 hours)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was successful in registering for all the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It is not rocket science; be on top of things and do what is expected of you.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Italian universities teach exclusively by lectures; there are no seminars. I knew this upon arrival. Though I am not keen on the Italian mode of teaching, I obviously had to accept this if I wanted to achieve my goal of studying Italian literature in Italy. Nevertheless it is an aspect of the programs that I must rate negatively.
Overall though all my courses were extremely interesting, I was only dissatisfied with the manner of teaching.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Because I wanted to study Italian literature in Italian, I choose courses that all included Italian texts. The challenge of the courses were not so much the course material but the fact that I am studying a subject for which I did not know the context upon arrival: Italian students obviously have some familiarity with Italian literature and history from their time at Liceo (high school). I had to gain this information in my free time by reading books on Italian literary history while also learning the language during the semester. In sum I would say that the level of the courses reflects the level at my own university in Denmark – it was only my choice to immerse myself in Italian that made the courses incredibly difficult.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: As already mentioned, the Italians only teach my lecturing (at least in the humanities). Each course consists of 60 hours of lecturing. On the one hand the student receives an incredible about of information to internalize during a semester, information which it is necessary to learn, since the exams are all oral. On the other the student does not develop the ability to think for herself, because the only requirement of the students is to learn exactly what the professor has said in lectures. In Copenhagen, the student has the opportunity to engage in a conversation with other students and professors in the seminars. Whereas the style of teaching in Italy is a monologue, the style at Copenhagen University is a dialogue. I certainly prefer the latter mode of teaching. Long live the Humboldt brothers who developed the seminar mode of teaching a few centuries ago in Berlin!

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 2 semesters

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Contemporary Italian Literature ("Occasione" of Eugenio Montale; "Alcyone" of D'Annunzio)
Italian Literature 1 (10 canti of Dante; 10 novellas from Boccaccio's "Decameron"; Tarchetti's "Fosca"; "La divina commedia" di Pasolini; "Il primo dio" by Emanuel Carnevale)

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
questions.answer:
Comparative Literature ("Oliver Twist" by Charles Dickens; "A Woman of 30" by Balzac; "Madame Bovary" by Flaubert; "The Turn of the Screw" by Henry James; "Wide Sargasso Sea" by Jean Rhys; "Aspects of the Novel" by Foster; a number of critical texts by Meneghelli and Barthes)
Italian Literature 2 ("Lezioni americane" and "Le cosmicomiche" by Calvino; "Il saggiatore" by Galileo; several canti from the divine comedy; Snow's "The Two Cultures"; )
Literary Theory ("Il barone rampante" by Calvino; "The red and the black" by Stendhal; "The Mill on the Floss" by George Eliot; "The American" by Henry James; "The Master of Ballantrae" by Stevenson; "The Grande Meaulnes" by Fournier; Critical Texts: "Letteratura. Teorie, metodi, strumenti" by Bertoni; "Teoria del romanzo" by Guido Mazzoni)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I highly recommend taking the three courses on Italian literature:
Italian Literature 1
Italian Literature 2
Contemporary Italian Literature
There is no better place in the world to study Italian literature than in Italy. Why waste your time with pseudo-courses taught in English in which you get a brief introduction to Italian literature when you can get the real deal? Be aware though that it is immensely time consuming to follow courses in Italian if you have never studied Italian literature before!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I mostly battled with inflation. Be aware that cheaper accommodation is available than what I chose; yet rents are constantly increasing in Bologna. Landlords typically add between 10 and 20 euros to the rent every six months.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: All items in supermarkets were about 10 % more expensive than I had expected. This was due to the severity of the inflation.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not take up any non-academic opportunities, because I had no time for it.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: N/A

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: N/A

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I recommend that they learn Italian, e.g. through sports activities or by following language classes at the university (I did the latter!). During my stay I met too many Erasmus students who could not even order a spritz in Italian. :-(

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I already knew Italy fairly well as I have many Italian friends and been on holiday in the country several times. Nevertheless it is always stressful to move to a new country. It is a challenge.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It was very difficult for me to localize with local students. The problems is that the universities offer activities specifically for erasmus students; at these activities you do not meet local students. At my courses it was also difficult to meet local students because lectures were 90 minutes without a break. In other words, there were no breaks that gave me the opportunity to socialize. I did meet some students, but it was challenging. Also, they tended not to invite me for anything; I had to seek the opportunities myself. It was tough. I recommend that exchange students install the application "tandem" on their phones in order to find Italian tandem partners; I met some Italians by using the application and got to know an Italian PhD student whom I met every week to practice my Italian.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The health care system is a challenge; I could not go to see a GP even with my private insurance, because the GPs do not offer a booking system that you can enter. In other words, legally I should be able to see a GP here; how to do it, I still have not figured out.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The Italian life style... Nothing better than a cup of coffee in the centre of beautiful Bologna!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Learn the language! The university offers you a course for free! You can take an intensive course that takes place in the two weeks preceding the start of the semester. And if possible, have a B2 Italian before arrival. It makes your stay much more rewarding!
2) Take courses in Italian. Even if you do not understand anything, why would you be in Italy to take a course in English? Then you might as well study in Dublin, where they speak a much better English!
3) Go to your lectures; too many Erasmus students on my course neglected the lectures; each course offers you 60 hours of spoken Italian. Who would want to miss this opportunity for learning the language?!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Consider taking two semesters abroad instead of one. None of the Erasmus students I knew wanted to go back after a single semester: they had just settled when they had to go back. What a shame!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The ability to sustain academic discussions for 40 minutes at my exams. For my first exam I was really nervous; at my second exam a professor told me to take as much time as I needed to express myself; this suggestion really helped. I am really proud that I managed to achieve a level of Italian in which I could complete five oral exams.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I chose to follow three courses on Italian literature. ALL the reading, both secondary and primary, was in Italian. I have never spent so much time on a single course in my life! The language barrier was therefore by far the biggest challenge. I recommend that students begin to learn the language well in advance before they begin their courses in Italy.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
I am grateful that University of Copenhagen do not write the grades that I achieved in Italy on my Danish transcript. It encouraged me to seek out courses that were taught in Italian, because I knew that a bad grade (owing to my lack of abilities in the Italian language!) would not be recorded on my transcript. Though I managed 3 top grades out of 5 exams, I also had a black-out at one exam, which resulted in a grade way below my usual level. The black out was entirely due to the language barrier; it would have been awful to have an unusually low grade on my transcript when this grade reflected more my capabilities in Italian than my knowledge of the subject. If the grades would be written on the transcript, I would obviously be more likely to choose courses in English than in Italian because that would play to my advantage.
I would however add that I hope that Copenhagen University encourage their students to take courses in Italian! It is very challenging but a very rewarding experience!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
